screens.title: Why debugging matters
screens.narratorSegment: Debugging is the process of locating, understanding, and fixing errors in your code. It differs from optimization: optimization makes correct code faster, while debugging makes faulty code correct. In practice, many development days are spent tracking down a single unexpected null or timing issue that breaks gameplay. Understanding this distinction helps prioritize work: fix correctness issues first so profiling and optimization are solving the real bottlenecks rather than hiding incorrect behavior. A concrete example is a player character that occasionally falls through geometry. Before spending cycles optimizing physics, reproduce and fix the root cause — perhaps a missing Rigidbody or an incorrect collision layer. A common misconception is that adding more logging will always help; excessive logging in update loops can flood the Console and obscure the real error while slowing the editor. Instead, prefer targeted logs, assertions, or breakpoints to capture the precise moment of failure. Your takeaway: reliable debugging habits prevent wasted optimization and help you ship correct features faster. Ask yourself: which bug would a short, well-placed assertion have revealed earlier? Why debugging matters means debugging ensures correctness; optimization improves performance. always confirm correctness before profiling.. In practical terms, debugging vs optimization — correctness before speed. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

What debugging is

screens.title: Message logging: Debug.Log family
screens.narratorSegment: Unity's Debug. Log family is the simplest way to see what's happening in your game. Use Debug. Log for general information like variable values or execution checkpoints. Use Debug. LogWarning for suspicious but non-fatal conditions you want to address, and Debug. LogError for severe issues that break functionality. Debug. Assert checks a boolean condition and logs an error and pauses execution in the Editor when the assertion fails, which is useful to catch violated assumptions early. A concrete example: before moving a target object, log whether the reference is null; if it is, log an error. Pair this with Debug. Assert to force a pause when a critical invariant is false. Beware of the common mistake of leaving many logs inside Update methods — printing every frame floods the Console and slows execution. If you need editor-only logging or gizmo drawing, wrap it with conditional compilation so it doesn't ship in a release build. Use logging sparingly and with clear messages and context so the Console trace leads you to the problem quickly. content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.6 › Message logging
Debug.Log family
Informational, warning, error, and assertions for runtime visibility.
• Debug.Log: general info and variable prints used for quick checks.
• Debug.LogWarning: highlight suspicious conditions that deserve attention but don't stop execution.
• Debug.LogError: show critical failures that often cause incorrect behavior or crashes.
• Debug.Assert: validate assumptions and pause the Editor when an important condition is false.
Common mistake
Leaving many logs in Update loops, which produces high-volume output and potential performance impact.
Code examples
// Informational
Debug.Log("Informational message.");

// Warning
Debug.LogWarning("Potential issue here!");

// Error
Debug.LogError("Critical error!");

// Assertion
Debug.Assert(playerRigidbody != null, "Player Rigidbody must be assigned");
Key Takeaway

Use the right level for clarity. Assertions help catch broken assumptions early in development.

screens.title: When to log vs when to set a breakpoint
screens.narratorSegment: Choosing between logging and breakpoints comes down to the type of question you need answered. Use logging when you want a persistent history of events across runs or when the issue is timing dependent and reproducing an exact pause is hard. Logs are also useful for remote diagnostics or for capturing a sequence of values leading to a failure. Use a breakpoint when you need to inspect the exact runtime state at a single point: the values of local variables, the call stack, or the result of evaluating an expression. For example, if a variable intermittently becomes null, a conditional breakpoint that pauses only when the variable is null lets you inspect how it got that value. A common misconception is that breakpoints are slower to use; in fact, breakpoints can be faster when they let you step through a problematic method instead of sifting through noisy logs. Your practical rule: start with a targeted log to confirm the bug, then attach the debugger and place a breakpoint where you need full state inspection. This combo reduces guesswork and helps you verify a fix quickly.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.6 › When to log vs breakpoint
Use Console logging
• Capture event sequences across frames. • Leave traces that persist after the run. • Good for remote diagnostics and automated runs.
Example: log positions of a spawned enemy over several frames to detect drift.
Common-mistake: logging every frame without gating or rate limiting.
Use IDE breakpoints
• Pause execution to inspect locals and call stack. • Step into methods to see the exact flow. • Use conditional breakpoints to pause only on specific values.
Example: set a breakpoint where a null reference occurs to see why the reference became null.
Pro tip: conditional breakpoints reduce noise when the condition is rare.
Key Takeaway

Start with a targeted log, then use a breakpoint for deep inspection if the issue persists.

screens.title: Using Visual Studio or VS Code to debug Unity
screens.narratorSegment: External IDE debuggers provide the most control over runtime inspection. The typical workflow begins by attaching the IDE to the Unity Editor. In Visual Studio choose Attach Unity Debugger and select the running Unity instance; in V S Code use the Attach to Unity Editor configuration. Once attached, set breakpoints by clicking the gutter next to a line of code. When execution reaches a breakpoint the editor pauses and highlights the line. Use Step Over to execute the current line without entering called methods, Step Into to follow a method call into its body, and Step Out to return from the current method. Continue resumes execution until the next breakpoint. While paused, inspect variables by hovering in the code, or by using the Locals and Watch windows to monitor specific values. The Call Stack shows how you reached this line, which is invaluable when an exception bubbles up through many methods. A common misconception is that breakpoints alter program timing in ways that hide bugs; while they can, the ability to observe exact state usually outweighs slight timing differences. Practice attaching your IDE, setting a breakpoint on the failing line, and watching how variables change as you step. How might you use a watch to confirm an assumption about a variable's value?

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.6 › IDE Debugging
Attach and Break
Attach your IDE to the running Unity Editor so breakpoints pause execution and reveal state.
1. Attach to Unity from your IDE.
2. Set breakpoints in the gutter on suspicious lines.
3. When paused: hover variables, check Locals, add Watches, inspect Call Stack.
Stepping Commands
Step Over (F10), Step Into (F11), Step Out (Shift+F11), Continue (F5).
Practical tip
Use Step Into when you suspect a method's internals; use Step Over when you trust called methods and want to move faster.
Locals
Shows local variables in the current scope.
Watch
Track specific expressions or variables across steps.
Call Stack
See the chain of method calls that led to the current line.

screens.title: NullReferenceException (NRE)
screens.narratorSegment: A NullReferenceException occurs when code attempts to access a member of an object that is null. In Unity this often happens when a field expected to be assigned in the Inspector is left empty, or when a runtime lookup fails. The typical symptom is a stack-trace pointing to a line like accessing transform or a component reference. For example, trying to call AddForce on a Rigidbody variable that wasn't assigned will throw an NRE. To prevent this, always check references before use or use explicit initialization. A defensive pattern is to check for null and log a helpful error or early return, which both documents the problem and prevents the exception from propagating. Another useful tool is Debug. Assert to catch violated invariants early during development. A frequent misconception is to assume the Inspector assignment persists across prefabs or scenes — verify references at runtime, especially when objects are instantiated dynamically. The practical habit is to add a null-check, informative error log, and a note in the Inspector or code comment explaining expected assignments. NullReferenceException (NRE) means an nre means you tried to use an object reference that is null. check assignments and guard before access.. In practical terms, understanding and preventing the most common c# runtime error in unity. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.6 › NullReferenceException
What causes an NRE
Accessing a member on a reference that is null. Common when inspector fields are not assigned or runtime finds fail.
Prevention tips:
  • Check for null before using a reference and log a clear message.
  • Use Debug.Assert to fail fast in the Editor when an invariant is violated.
  • Initialize references where possible and verify Inspector assignments.
Example scenario
public Rigidbody playerRigidbody; // left unassigned
void Update() {
  // This will throw a NullReferenceException if playerRigidbody is null
  playerRigidbody.AddForce(Vector3.up * jumpForce, ForceMode.Impulse);
}

// Safer:
void Update() {
  if (playerRigidbody == null) {
    Debug.LogWarning("Player Rigidbody is not assigned!");
    return;
  }
  playerRigidbody.AddForce(Vector3.up * jumpForce, ForceMode.Impulse);
}
Key Takeaway

Guard references and prefer clear logs or assertions to catch missing assignments early.

screens.title: IndexOutOfRangeException & argument errors
screens.narratorSegment: IndexOutOfRangeException occurs when code accesses an array or list at an index outside its valid range. This often happens when iterating with incorrect bounds or when assumptions about collection size are wrong. For example, accessing element ten of a five-element array will raise this exception. Prevent it by validating indices before use and by using safe iteration patterns such as foreach where appropriate. ArgumentNullException and ArgumentOutOfRangeException are related: they occur when methods receive invalid inputs. Check parameters at method entry and provide clear error logs or throw explicit exceptions when preconditions are violated. A common misconception is that these errors only appear in exotic edge cases; in practice they reveal incorrect assumptions about data shapes or timing, such as expecting a list to have been populated before access. Use defensive coding: check collection lengths, validate inputs, and add logs that print collection sizes when an unexpected index is used. This practice makes reproducing and fixing the cause much faster. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.6 › Index & Argument Errors
IndexOutOfRangeException
Occurs when accessing an index outside a collection's bounds. Validate counts and prefer safe loops.
Prevention:
  • Check index < collection.Count before access.
  • Use foreach when you don't need an index.
  • Log collection sizes when unexpected indices occur.
Argument exceptions
Throw or log clear messages when methods receive invalid arguments so callers know what's wrong.
if (index < 0 || index >= myList.Count) {
  Debug.LogError("Invalid index " + index + " for list of size " + myList.Count);
  return;
}
Key Takeaway

Validate indices and arguments at method entry. Clear logs make reproducing errors faster.

screens.title: BuggyPlayer walkthrough — find and fix a NullReferenceException
screens.narratorSegment: We will walk through the provided BuggyPlayer script to reproduce and fix a NullReferenceException. First, run the scene with the script attached and leave the public Rigidbody field unassigned. Buggy script (starter)
// BuggyPlayer.cs
using UnityEngine;

public class BuggyPlayer : MonoBehaviour
{
    public Rigidbody playerRigidbody; // Intentionally left unassigned
    public float jumpForce = 5f;
    private string playerName = "Hero";

    void Update()
    {
        if (Input.GetKeyDown(KeyCode.Space))
        {
            // This line will cause a NullReferenceException if playerRigidbody is not assigned
            playerRigidbody.AddForce(Vector3.up * jumpForce, ForceMode.Impulse);
            Debug.Log("Player " + playerName + " attempted to jump.");
        }
    }

    void OnCollisionEnter(Collision collision)
    {
        Debug.Log("Player collided with: " + collision.gameObject.name);
    }
}

screens.title: Conditional compilation: #if UNITY_EDITOR
screens.narratorSegment: Conditional compilation directives allow you to include code only in specific build targets. In Unity, wrapping debug-only code with #if UNITY_EDITOR ensures that the enclosed code is compiled only for the Editor and not included in standalone builds. This is important for editor tooling or heavy debug visualizations that would otherwise bloat your final player or impact performance. For example, debug drawing or editor gizmo utilities should be protected with #if UNITY_EDITOR to avoid shipping them. An alternative is relying on the engine's stripping of Debug. Log calls in non-development builds, but that is not guaranteed for custom tools and does not remove other debug behavior. A common misconception is that using if (Application. isEditor) is equivalent; it is not: Application. isEditor is evaluated at runtime and the code still compiles into the build, adding size and potential performance costs. Use #if UNITY_EDITOR for compile-time exclusion when you want code to be absent entirely from release binaries. Test your build configuration to be sure the code is stripped as expected. screens.title: Systematic debugging strategies
screens.narratorSegment: Systematic debugging turns a chaotic investigation into a sequence of repeatable experiments. Start by reproducing the bug reliably — if you cannot make it happen consistently, simplify conditions until you can. Next isolate the failing subsystem by removing unrelated systems or creating a minimal scene. Use divide-and-conquer: comment out or bypass parts of the code until the problem disappears, then add back sections to find the exact culprit. Use targeted logging or a breakpoint at the suspect line to inspect state and verify assumptions. Always check your assumptions: did you expect a component to be assigned, or a callback to run before another? Reading the stack trace will point you to the calling chain and often reveals which function invoked the failing code. When you find a fix, verify it with the minimal reproduction and then test the broader scene to ensure you didn't hide other side effects. Finally, document the root cause and the fix so future developers learn the lesson. This disciplined approach reduces time spent guessing and increases confidence in the fix. fullNarratorScript:
Debugging is the daily craft of a game programmer. In this lesson you will learn core approaches that make bugs visible and manageable: message logging with Unity's Debug methods, using an external IDE debugger to pause and inspect execution, and applying conditional compilation so debugging helpers don't end up in your release build. You will also practice handling the most common C# errors in Unity, such as null-reference and out-of-range access, and build a repeatable approach to reproduce and isolate problems. For example, using Debug. LogError to capture a failing object reference combined with a breakpoint in Visual Studio gives you both a permanent trace and the ability to see the exact runtime state. This chapter matters because a fast game that crashes or behaves unpredictably is unusable; solid debugging practices turn intermittent crashes into clear, fixable steps. As you move through the screens you'll see short code examples, a hands-on buggy script to reproduce a null reference, and a set of strategies you can reuse. Consider: what small check could have stopped your last bug earlier?

By the end of this chapter you will be able to use Unity's built-in logging and assertion tools to record program behavior, and to reason about when to use each. You will learn to set up and use an external debugger such as Visual Studio or V S Code to attach to the running Unity Editor, place breakpoints, step through execution, and inspect variables and call stacks. These debugging skills let you move from guessing at causes to seeing exact runtime state. We will also cover conditional compilation directives that avoid shipping debug helpers into release builds, an important performance consideration. Each objective includes a short practical mnemonic so you can recall which tool to use when a problem appears. Practice these skills on a small buggy script to connect the tools with real fixes.

This second objectives screen zooms into the practical subskills you will use. You will learn how to reproduce a bug reliably, a crucial first step before attempting a fix. You will practice isolating the failing code by creating minimal scenes or commenting out unrelated systems so the problem becomes obvious. You will also develop a divide-and-conquer approach to narrow down which line or block causes the issue. Finally, you will practice reading and interpreting stack traces so that the console message points you to the exact file and line. Each of these skills turns chaotic debugging into a repeatable investigation. In the hands-on activity we provide a buggy script that triggers a null reference and an out-of-range access so you can practice logging, breakpoints, and systematic isolation together. Learning Objectives — Practical Skills means reproduce bugs reliably, isolate the cause, and use breakpoints and stack traces to identify the exact failing line.. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Debugging is the process of locating, understanding, and fixing errors in your code. It differs from optimization: optimization makes correct code faster, while debugging makes faulty code correct. In practice, many development days are spent tracking down a single unexpected null or timing issue that breaks gameplay. Understanding this distinction helps prioritize work: fix correctness issues first so profiling and optimization are solving the real bottlenecks rather than hiding incorrect behavior. A concrete example is a player character that occasionally falls through geometry. Before spending cycles optimizing physics, reproduce and fix the root cause — perhaps a missing Rigidbody or an incorrect collision layer. Choosing between logging and breakpoints comes down to the type of question you need answered. Use logging when you want a persistent history of events across runs or when the issue is timing dependent and reproducing an exact pause is hard. Logs are also useful for remote diagnostics or for capturing a sequence of values leading to a failure.
